title: Rigveda 4.14: To Indra
source: Penn Ms. Coll. 390 Item 41 (undated (catalogued with Penn's 18th-19th c. Vedic manuscripts)), OPenn, Public Domain Mark + Aufrecht's accented text (GRETIL) + Griffith's English (VedaWeb)
description: Rigveda 4.14: To Indra: Sanskrit text and Griffith's English, each verse linked to the page of an undated Rigveda manuscript (Penn Ms. Coll. 390 Item 41) that carries it.
introduction:
Rigveda 4.14 is a hymn of 5 verses addressed to Indra. It stands in book (maṇḍala) 4, the family book of Vāmadeva. The Rigveda is the oldest collection of Sanskrit hymns, composed in the second half of the second millennium BCE and handed down orally for many centuries before it was written down.

The manuscript shown is Penn Ms. Coll. 390 Item 41 (University of Pennsylvania), an undated paper manuscript of the padapāṭha (the word-by-word recitation text, in which every word is written separately and compounds are split) of the whole Ṛgveda in Devanāgarī, 884 leaves in fascicles, 7-9 lines to the page, accents in red; this hymn stands on fol. 268r-268v. Each section below gives the verses that end on one page; the page boundaries were read on the images (the opening words of every page), not counted out. Where the manuscript is a padapāṭha (the word-by-word recitation text), the section shows Aufrecht's continuous (saṃhitā) text first and, as the edition text, the padapāṭha of the same verses, which is the form written on the page.
translator_notes: Sanskrit: Aufrecht's edition (1877) with the Vedic accents, as entered by van Nooten and Holland (GRETIL).

English: Ralph T. H. Griffith, The Hymns of the Rigveda (1889-1892; 2nd ed. 1896-1897), from the VedaWeb digital text; OCR slips in that text were corrected against the printed 2nd edition (data/sources/rigveda/griffith_errata.json).
Padapāṭha (edition text): Sansknet e-text via GRETIL (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0).

translation.original_ref: RV 4.14.1-5 (aṣṭaka 3, adhyāya 5, varga 14); Penn Ms. Coll. 390 Item 41 fol. 268v
translation.original_text:
1praty a̱gnir u̱ṣaso̍ jā̱tave̍dā̱ akhya̍d de̱vo roca̍mānā̱ maho̍bhiḥ | ā nā̍satyorugā̱yā rathe̍ne̱maṁ ya̱jñam upa̍ no yāta̱m accha̍ ||
2ū̱rdhvaṁ ke̱tuṁ sa̍vi̱tā de̱vo a̍śre̱j jyoti̱r viśva̍smai̱ bhuva̍nāya kṛ̱ṇvan | āprā̱ dyāvā̍pṛthi̱vī a̱ntari̍kṣa̱ṁ vi sūryo̍ ra̱śmibhi̱ś ceki̍tānaḥ ||
3ā̱vaha̍nty aru̱ṇīr jyoti̱ṣāgā̍n ma̱hī ci̱trā ra̱śmibhi̱ś ceki̍tānā | pra̱bo̱dhaya̍ntī suvi̱tāya̍ de̱vy u1̱̍ṣā ī̍yate su̱yujā̱ rathe̍na ||
4ā vā̱ṁ vahi̍ṣṭhā i̱ha te va̍hantu̱ rathā̱ aśvā̍sa u̱ṣaso̱ vyu̍ṣṭau | i̱me hi vā̍m madhu̱peyā̍ya̱ somā̍ a̱smin ya̱jñe vṛ̍ṣaṇā mādayethām ||
5anā̍yato̱ ani̍baddhaḥ ka̱thāyaṁ nya̍ṅṅ uttā̱no 'va̍ padyate̱ na | kayā̍ yāti sva̱dhayā̱ ko da̍darśa di̱vaḥ ska̱mbhaḥ samṛ̍taḥ pāti̱ nāka̍m ||
translation.text:
1THE God hath looked, even Agni Jâtavedas, to meet the Dawns refulgent in their glories. Come on your chariot, ye who travel widely, come to this sacrifice of ours, Nâsatyas.
2Producing light for all the world of creatures, God Savitar hath raised aloft his banner. Making his presence known by sunbeams, Sûrya hath filled the firmament and earth and heaven.
3Red Dawn.is come, riding with brightness onward, distinguished by her beams, gay-hued and mighty. Dawn on her nobly-harnessed car, the Goddess, awaking men to happiness, approacheth.
4May those most powerful steeds and chariot bring you, O Aṣvins, hither at the break of morning. Here for your draught of meath are Soma juices: at this our sacrifice rejoice, ye Mighty.
5How is it that, unbound and unsupported, he falleth not although directed downward? By what self-power moves he? Who hath seen it? He guards the vault of heaven, a close-set pillar?
translation.scan_note: Penn Ms. Coll. 390 Item 41, fol. 268v (numbered 77v by the scribe) (OPenn image 269, upper leaf). Checked on the image: the Rigveda text on this page begins in RV 4.14.1 ‹-agniḥ uṣasaḥ jāta-vedāḥ akhyat›. The next page with Rigveda text, fol. 269r (numbered 78r by the scribe), begins in RV 4.15.1 ‹-nīyate devaḥ deveṣu yajñiyaḥ›. Verses 4.14.1-5 end on this page; 4.14.1 begins on fol. 268r (numbered 77r by the scribe).
